attestations.source_text: There are many types of pronouns in French. Let’s start with the subject pronouns you have already used when conjugating verbs.
VOCABULAIRE
Another type of pronoun is the direct object pronoun (le pronom objet direct).
Now that you have mastered the pronom objet direct, let’s take a look at the pronom objet indirect (indirect object pronoun).
Y is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb.
En is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb.

When a direct and indirect pronoun appear in the same sentence, the indirect object pronoun comes first, unless the direct and indirect pronouns are in the third person, in which case the direct object pronoun comes first.
There are many ways to use disjunctive pronouns, also known as stressed or tonic pronouns.

grammar_rules.summary: The subject pronouns in French are je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles.
grammar_rules.explanation: Subject pronouns replace subject nouns. The third-person pronouns apply to people, animals, or things.
grammar_rules.formation: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles
usage: Used as the subject of a verb.

attestations.source_text: je I; tu you (singular familiar); il he, it (masculine); elle she, it (feminine); on one, we, they, people; nous we; vous you (singular formal and all plurals); ils they (masculine, or mixed masculine and feminine); elles they (feminine)

grammar_rules.summary: Use tu with friends, family, children, animals; use vous with strangers or to maintain distance/respect. Contemporary trend is toward familiarity among peers.
grammar_rules.explanation: Tu is informal; vous is formal or plural.
usage: Addressing friends, family, children, animals with tu.
Addressing strangers or showing respect with vous.
restrictions: Let the native speaker initiate first exchange with tu.
common_traps: Using tu when vous is appropriate can be perceived as rude.

attestations.source_text: Use tu and its verb forms to talk to friends, family members, children, and animals. Use vous when you are addressing a stranger or someone you don’t know well, or to maintain a certain degree of distance or respect.

grammar_rules.summary: On can mean one, we, they, or people in general; it can also replace a passive voice.
grammar_rules.explanation: On has multiple meanings depending on context: indefinite person, general people, informal nous, informal tu, and passive equivalent.
usage: Indefinite person: On voudrait tout réussir.
People in general: En France, on boit du vin.
Informal nous: On va au cinéma cet après-midi?
Informal tu: Alors, on se promène au lieu de faire ses devoirs!
common_traps: Distinguish between the different meanings of on based on context.

attestations.source_text: The pronoun on has several meanings.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Direct object pronouns forms and placement
grammar_rules.summary: Direct object pronouns: me (m'), te (t'), le (l'), la (l'), nous, vous, les. They precede the conjugated verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: They replace direct object nouns (no preposition). They agree in gender and number with the noun replaced. They precede the verb to which they refer.
grammar_rules.formation: me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les (with elision before vowels/mute h)
usage: Precede the conjugated verb (or auxiliary in compound tenses).
restrictions: Can replace nouns with definite article, possessive adjective, or demonstrative adjective.
agreement_rules: In compound tenses, past participle agrees with preceding direct object pronoun.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: pronoun + verb + subject? (inversion) Actually: pronoun + verb + hyphen + subject pronoun.
transformations: Me/m' and te/t' become moi/toi in affirmative imperative.
common_traps: Don't confuse le/la/les with articles; they are pronouns.
Remember elision before vowels and mute h.

attestations.source_text: SINGULAR PLURAL; me (m') me; te (t') you (familiar); le (l') him or it (masculine); la (l') her or it (feminine); nous us; vous you (plural or formal); les them (masc. and fem.)

grammar_rules.rule_name: Direct object pronouns in compound tenses
grammar_rules.summary: In passé composé, the direct object pronoun precedes the auxiliary verb; past participle agrees in gender and number with the preceding direct object.
grammar_rules.explanation: The pronoun is placed before the auxiliary (avoir/être). Past participle agrees with the direct object pronoun.
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees in gender and number when direct object precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + pronoun + auxiliary + pas + past participle
common_traps: Do not confuse with indirect object pronoun which does not cause agreement.

attestations.source_text: In the passé composé and other compound tenses, the direct object pronoun is placed before the auxiliary verb. The past participle agrees in number and gender when the direct object precedes the verb.

grammar_rules.summary: In affirmative imperative, the pronoun follows the verb and is linked by a hyphen; me/te become moi/toi. In negative imperative, the pronoun precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: Affirmative: verb-pronoun. Negative: ne pronoun verb pas.
grammar_rules.formation: Affirmative: verb + hyphen + pronoun (moi/toi). Negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.
common_traps: Remember the hyphen in affirmative imperative.

attestations.source_text: In the affirmative imperative, the direct object pronoun follows the verb. Me (m’) and te (t’) change to moi and toi. Remember to link the verb to the pronoun with a hyphen. In the negative imperative, the direct object pronoun remains before the verb.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Indirect object pronouns forms and placement
grammar_rules.summary: Indirect object pronouns: me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. They precede the conjugated verb; no past participle agreement.
grammar_rules.explanation: Replace animate indirect objects (people/animals). The object is indirect when controlled by a preposition (parler à, répondre à, écrire à).
grammar_rules.formation: me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur (elision before vowels/mute h)
restrictions: Only for animate objects; inanimate objects use y or en.
agreement_rules: Past participle never agrees with an indirect object pronoun.
transformations: me -> moi, te -> toi in affirmative imperative.

attestations.source_text: SINGULAR PLURAL; me (m’) me; te (t’) you (familiar); lui him, her; nous us; vous you (formal or plural); leur them (masc. and fem.)

grammar_rules.summary: In affirmative imperative, pronoun follows verb with hyphen; me/te become moi/toi. In negative imperative, pronoun precedes verb.
grammar_rules.formation: Affirmative: verb + pronoun (moi/toi). Negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.

attestations.source_text: In the affirmative imperative, the indirect object pronoun follows the verb. Me (m’) and te (t’) become moi and toi. Remember to link the verb to the following pronoun with a hyphen. In the negative imperative, the indirect object pronoun remains before the verb.

grammar_rules.summary: Y replaces inanimate object preceded by à or sur. It precedes the verb; no past participle agreement.
grammar_rules.explanation: Y is an indirect object pronoun that replaces things/ideas introduced by à (sometimes sur).
usage: Replace sur + inanimate noun in some cases.
restrictions: Does not replace people (use disjunctive pronouns).
agreement_rules: No past participle agreement with y.
grammar_rules.word_order: y + verb (or y + auxiliary + past participle)
common_traps: Do not use y for people; use disjunctive pronouns after preposition.

attestations.source_text: Y is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb. It usually replaces an inanimate object (thing or idea). The object replaced by y is considered indirect because it is preceded by a preposition, usually the preposition à, but sometimes sur.

grammar_rules.summary: En replaces inanimate object preceded by de. It precedes the verb; no past participle agreement.
grammar_rules.explanation: En is an indirect object pronoun replacing things/ideas introduced by de.
restrictions: Does not replace people (use disjunctive pronouns).
agreement_rules: No past participle agreement with en.
grammar_rules.word_order: en + verb (or en + auxiliary + past participle)
common_traps: Do not confuse with y (à vs de).

attestations.source_text: En is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb. It usually replaces an inanimate object (thing or idea) preceded by de.

grammar_rules.summary: When two object pronouns occur together, the indirect comes first unless both are third person, in which case direct comes first.
grammar_rules.explanation: Order: me/te/nous/vous before le/la/les; le/la/les before lui/leur; en always in second position.
grammar_rules.formation: me/te/nous/vous + le/la/les; le/la/les + lui/leur; indirect + en
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees with preceding direct object pronoun, not with en or indirect pronouns.
common_traps: Remember that third person direct object comes before third person indirect object.

attestations.source_text: When a direct and indirect pronoun appear in the same sentence, the indirect object pronoun comes first, unless the direct and indirect pronouns are in the third person, in which case the direct object pronoun comes first.

grammar_rules.summary: Disjunctive pronouns: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.
grammar_rules.explanation: Stressed/tonic pronouns used in various contexts.
grammar_rules.formation: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles
usage: Emphasis, after prepositions, comparisons, isolation, etc.

attestations.source_text: moi me; toi you; lui him; elle her; nous us; vous you; eux them; elles them (feminine)

grammar_rules.rule_name: Disjunctive pronouns with verbs taking à/de + person
grammar_rules.summary: When a verb takes à or de before an animate object, the disjunctive pronoun is used (lui, elle, eux, elles) instead of y/en.
grammar_rules.explanation: Contrast: y/en for things, disjunctive for people.
common_traps: Using y/en for people is incorrect.

attestations.source_text: Disjunctive pronouns are used with certain verbs when the indirect object is a person. Compare: Je parle de ce film. J’en parle. and Je parle de ce metteur en scène. Je parle de lui.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement with object pronouns
exceptions_and_traps.description: The past participle agrees with a preceding direct object pronoun, but never with an indirect object pronoun (including y and en).
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Le journaliste les a prises. (direct object feminine plural)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Le journaliste leur a parlés. (indirect object)

attestations.source_text: The past participle agrees in number and gender when the direct object precedes the verb.
the past participle never agrees with an indirect object pronoun

exceptions_and_traps.title: Using y/en for people
exceptions_and_traps.description: Y and en replace inanimate objects. For people, use disjunctive pronouns after the preposition.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: J'en parle (when referring to a person).

attestations.source_text: Disjunctive pronouns are used with certain verbs when the indirect object is a person.
